findings.exactExcerpt: The Greek New Testament has a striking phrase that appears nine times in the Pastoral Epistles (1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus) and almost nowhere else. The phrase is *hygiainousa didaskalia* — *sound* or *healthy doctrine*.
findings.problem: The opening hook claims the phrase *hygiainousa didaskalia* appears nine times in the Pastoral Epistles. The article's own later list gives four passages (1 Timothy 1:10; 2 Timothy 4:3; Titus 1:9; 2:1), and the pinned Nestle 1904 morphology confirms the adjective–noun pairing occurs in exactly those four verses. Even the looser counts fail: the adjective ὑγιαίνω in any Pastoral collocation occurs 8 times (1 Tim 1:10; 6:3; 2 Tim 1:13; 4:3; Titus 1:9; 1:13; 2:1; 2:2), and both words in the same verse 5 times. No defensible counting of the named phrase yields nine.

localEvidence.observation: Claim of nine occurrences of the phrase.

localEvidence.locator: later section, “Sound or healthy teaching” paragraph
localEvidence.observation: The article itself lists exactly four passages: “1 Timothy 1:10 (sound doctrine), 2 Timothy 4:3 (sound teaching), Titus 1:9, 2:1 (sound doctrine)” — contradicting the opening claim.
Co-occurrence in the same verse: 1Tim 1:10, 6:3; 2Tim 4:3; Titus 1:9; 2:1 (5 verses); grammatical adjective–noun pairing in 4 of them (1Tim 6:3 has ὑγιαίνω modifying λόγοις).

findings.claimScope: article-opening quantitative claim about the named phrase
findings.plausibleAlternative: The author may have meant every “sound/healthy” word-group occurrence in the Pastorals; that count is 8 (ὑγιαίνω), still not nine.
findings.suggestedMinimalCorrection: Change “nine times” to “four times” (1 Timothy 1:10; 2 Timothy 4:3; Titus 1:9; 2:1), matching the article's own later list.

findings.exactExcerpt: treating Christ as “is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation. All things were created through Him and for Him.” (v. 15)
findings.problem: Cluster of quotation-boundary defects around Colossians 1:15–17. (a) Two adjacent quotations are grammatically broken at the seam — “treating Christ as ‘is the image…’” and “After calling Christ ‘is the image…’” — the quoted text begins with a verb phrase that cannot complete the sentence frame. (b) The quotation labeled “(v. 15)” runs through “All things were created through Him and for Him,” which is the text of verse 16. (c) The immediately following sentence attributes the same wording again to “verse 16,” repeating the same BSB text verbatim (“The Son is the image… All things were created through Him and for Him. He is before all things…”), so one block of Scripture is duplicated across two adjacent quotations with shifted verse labels.

“All things were created through Him and for Him” belongs to verse 16, not verse 15, in the BSB text.

findings.suggestedMinimalCorrection: Reframe as: Christ “is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation” (v. 15); then quote the v. 16 text once under its own label, removing the duplicated quotation.

findings.exactExcerpt: The etymology runs from a verbal root meaning "to bind together" or "to join." Peace, in the Greek conception, is what holds parties together
findings.problem: The derivation of εἰρήνη from a root meaning “to bind together / to join” (i.e., εἴρω) is stated as fact, but the standard etymological references treat the etymology of εἰρήνη as uncertain (Beekes registers it as without established etymology, possibly Pre-Greek). The sentence then leverages the asserted root to supply the “Greek conception” of peace — the etymology-supplies-meaning pattern this audit is charged to flag.

localEvidence.observation: Unhedged etymology claim followed immediately by a meaning claim built on it (“Peace, in the Greek conception, is what holds parties together”).
No hedging language (“possibly,” “often connected with”) is present, unlike the packet's careful treatments elsewhere (e.g., hyios notes that lexicographers debate the etymology).

findings.plausibleAlternative: The εἴρω connection is a real, older scholarly proposal (so the claim is not invented), but it is one hypothesis and is doubted by current etymological dictionaries.
findings.suggestedMinimalCorrection: Hedge and detach meaning from etymology: “The etymology is uncertain; the word has traditionally been connected with εἴρω, ‘to join,’ though modern etymological dictionaries doubt the derivation. In usage, …”

localEvidence.observation: Unhedged etymology claim followed by a meaning claim built on it.
